item.title: Quad9 (DNS Resolver) to Exit France
item.description:
Source: quad9.net

Top Comment:

(context: I'm the CTO of Quad9 and am one of the people dealing with the lawyers)

There is an understandable focus on "how are you going to block French users" when we have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names - we understand this conflict, but we think it is energy spent in the wrong place.

It is probable that we will use geoIP filters to block French users from our services after November 24. We could apply this same geoIP filter list now to selectively block French users from reaching the sites that we've been told to make unavailable. But this would corrupt our core premise, which is that the DNS is not the right place for this to happen, and if we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users and we still do not have legally perfect coverage. We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission, and secondarily we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us. By accepting the demands for blocking, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we will act on behalf of companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint.

We would be admitting that we think this solves the problem - it does not. We would be admitting that we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names - we will not. We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons - we must not.

So we accept that there is the possibility that we will have errors in our blockade, but in this case (blocking French users) we maintain consistency with our stated mission of integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you get the DNS as you (the user) expects, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all.

The underlying issue is not ONLY that geoIP blocking is ineffective, but that the entire premise of any of these demands is inappropriately applied to DNS recursive resolution providers. We would hope that this discussion continues to be on the most fundamental of the disagreement we have with the outcome in this court case, not on the details of the technical implementation which have yet to be entirely decided and which can be tuned over time.

item.description:

I am truly sorry. I take full responsibility for my actions.

It was not remotely my intention to cause any of the subsequent side effects.

At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing.

As someone who follows the 4-weekly PHP release cycle and compiles it from source, my intention was to alert others in a similar position to be aware of the importance/urgency of the updates.

That clearly backfired in a pretty wild fashion. I have learned my lesson.

Top Comment:

> At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing.

If you're not a party to an embargo, and no one told you an embargo even exists... you should not follow the embargo. In fact, you should maybe even consider leaking basic details or challenging the embargo if you are in this situation. In your situation, they had lost information asymmetry before the news got to you. I don't know where people got the idea that unrelated third parties have to follow embargos.

Embargos are not about keeping secrets, they are about the game theory of coordinated disclosure.

item.title: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

I've been using iron proxy recently for a project I just started, it does network restrictions by domain etc with plenty of options, credential swapping and more.

I have no affiliation with it, but it solved most of what I need in one go when I was stressing out about it.

Only real problem remaining if you truly want to be able to trust agents is how to prevent data (in my case codebases the agent works on) exfiltration a la HF incident.

We can restrict network to trusted domains, but there's always a chance an agent could be extra slippery especially if prompt injected and doing something like pushing data out a few characters at a time.

In my case I'm also giving it gh access and having to deeply check things like: can it manage to fork public repos and embarrass us by submitting prs, could it open issues, etc.

But that's kind of solved by proxying the heck out of gh rather than giving it direct (or wrapping it or whatever) for additional controls that gh themselves don't provide.

I'm still musing over the "it could send data to an allowed domain in a way we don't expect that exfiltrates something"...

item.title: OpenAI CLI
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

For a site focused on technical users, seems like a lot of people in this thread are completely lost at the idea that a single service may offer multiple pieces of software dedicated to specific use-cases.

codex: OpenAI's agent harness. The thing you typically want to interact with when you want an agent powered by OpenAI models to do stuff on your machine. Abstracts the low-level functionality of their API so you don't have to worry about it.

openai-cli: A simple CLI exposing low-level operations against OpenAI's REST API. The thing you'd use for creating lower-level scripts to directly call the completions API, administer accounts, etc.

Honestly, this is obvious by the name alone. If it's not clear to you, then this isn't for you. No need to get worked up about OpenAI releasing a piece of software where you're not the audience.
